query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: At 600 ± 25 °C in ambient air, the dominant factor governing both macroscopic wear rate and microscopic subsurface deformation of an equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy (HEA) coating is the in-situ formation of a continuous, nanocrystalline Cr-rich spinel oxide (∼50–150 nm thick). If the continuity of this oxide is disrupted so that its area coverage falls below ≈70 %, the coating will exhibit (i) at least twice the volumetric wear loss and (ii) a deeper plastic‐deformation zone (by ≥40 %) under identical sliding conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: 5 µm-thick equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu coating deposited by magnetron sputtering on AISI 304 substrate; as-deposited, single-phase fcc, grain size 50–100 nm, surface roughness Ra ≈ 20 nm.
generation.intervention: Reduce ambient oxygen partial pressure during sliding from air (21 kPa O₂) to low-oxygen Ar–1 vol %O₂ atmosphere, keeping all other parameters constant. This impedes rapid formation of the continuous Cr-rich spinel layer.
generation.conditions: Pin-on-disk sliding, alumina counter-body, 5 N normal load, 0.1 m s⁻¹ sliding speed, 600 °C, 30 min duration.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous nanocrystalline Cr-rich spinel (Fe,Ni)(Cr,Co)₂O₄ layer covering ≥70 % of the contact surface.
generation.mechanism: In air, fast outward diffusion of Cr and Co during sliding oxidation forms a lubricious, hard spinel layer that (1) carries a large share of the contact load, (2) shields the underlying metallic coating from adhesive junction formation, and (3) suppresses subsurface shear localization. Lower O₂ suppresses or discontinuously breaks this layer, exposing softer metallic asperities that undergo severe plastic flow and adhesive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the air (baseline) test, sliding in Ar–1 % O₂ will (a) increase the specific wear rate by ≈100 % (±30 %) and (b) increase the depth of the plastically deformed subsurface zone from ≈0.7 µm to ≥1.0 µm, as measured by focused-ion-beam cross-sections.
generation.baseline: In air at 600 °C the coating exhibits a specific wear rate of (3 ± 0.5) × 10⁻⁵ mm³ N⁻¹ m⁻¹ and a plastic zone depth of 0.7 ± 0.1 µm; surface analysis shows a ≥70 % coverage of a 50–150 nm Cr-rich spinel film.
generation.boundary: Applies to 500–650 °C, normal loads 2–10 N, equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu coatings 3–10 µm thick on austenitic stainless substrates, and counter-bodies that do not themselves supply oxygen or form glassy tribofilms.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of the critical 70 % coverage threshold and exact wear-rate doubling may vary with coating thickness and grain size; lack of prior systematic data on Cu segregation in this HEA introduces additional uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two identical coated coupons. Slide one in air (baseline) and one in Ar–1 % O₂ at 600 °C under the defined conditions. Characterize post-test surfaces by TEM cross-section, XPS mapping, and 3D profilometry.
measurements: Depth of plastically deformed subsurface zone (µm)
Area fraction of continuous spinel oxide (%)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the low-oxygen sample either (a) retains ≥70 % continuous spinel coverage yet shows ≥2× higher wear OR (b) exhibits <70 % coverage but wear rate increases by <25 % and plastic zone depth rises by <10 % relative to baseline.
